title: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I nevertheless suspect that even when much more realistic models for specific materials are used, the fundamental mechanisms responsible for randomness will still be very much the same as in the extremely simple model shown here.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “The Breaking of Materials” (from p. 374), p. 375. Scope: fracture of solids, from single crystals to geological faults

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fracture roughness and displacement fields are standard observables, and some public datasets exist. The broad material-independence and causal exclusion of irregularities are much harder to test than roughness itself. Current data support restricted comparisons but not the full scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Analyze crack trajectories and displacement fields in specimens with independently mapped heterogeneity, comparing deterministic fracture models with heterogeneity-driven models across material classes and scales. A material-independent residual roughness law predicted by the interaction model would support the claim; strong dependence on mapped disorder would oppose it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar roughness exponents can arise from different mechanisms.

Coverage from crystals to geological faults is inadequate.

Microscopic material disorder is difficult to measure completely before fracture.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fracture-roughness exponents and the contrast between cleavage and intergranular failure are published and partly public, and fault catalogs cover the large-scale end. Those data can reject a claim of universal roughness independent of material. They do not identify one deterministic cellular-automaton mechanism as the common cause across that range.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare roughness statistics of fracture surfaces in single crystals, polycrystals, and mapped geological faults, and test whether a material-free displacement rule reproduces those statistics better than a model driven by pre-existing flaws. Equally rough single-crystal fractures, with the same exponents as faults, would support a material-independent mechanism; smooth cleavage, or roughness that tracks grain boundaries, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Single-crystal cleavage is often smooth on favored planes, so the sample of breaks is biased toward rough ones.

Matching a cellular-automaton picture does not show that the same mechanism operates from silicon to faults.

fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.65
